Key sentences:
- “The ongoing public health crisis will continue to weigh on economic activity, employment, and inflation in the near term, and poses considerable risks to the economic outlook over the medium term.”
- “With inflation running persistently below this longer-run goal, the Committee will aim to achieve inflation moderately above 2 percent for some time… [and] expects to maintain an accommodative stance of monetary policy until these outcomes are achieved.”

Literature-informed rationale:
- COVID-19 has raised economic policy uncertainty and generated combined demand and supply-chain shocks, historically associated with downside risks to activity (pandemic-induced EPU and shock literature). This supports a negative baseline tone.
- At the zero lower bound, forward guidance and quantitative easing—explicitly noted here via Treasury and agency MBS purchases and policy directives—work through expectations and term premia to ease financial conditions (Fed literature on forward guidance/QE; influence on long-term rates and expected inflation). This tempers the negativity.
- The Fed’s shift to average inflation targeting (makeup strategy) is consistent with theory emphasizing the expectations channel and the Taylor principle: committing to allow inflation to moderately exceed 2% can lower real rates and better anchor expectations at target (Clarida/Taylor principle; AIT announced at Jackson Hole 2020). That reduces deflation risk implied by weak demand and low oil prices’ drag on inflation.
- The Phillips-curve evidence in recent years suggests muted inflation response to slack; combined with virus-related uncertainty, this keeps disinflationary pressure salient despite accommodation, preventing a neutral or positive tone.
Netting these, the statement remains moderately negative but less so than a purely risk-focused reading.
